blocks.html: When the Civil War and Reconstruction ended, the country turned west. The tool that opened the West fastest was the railroad. Before 1869, going from the East Coast to California took months by wagon or by ship. After 1869 it took about a week.

blocks.cap: The two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah Territory. The Central Pacific built east from Sacramento; the Union Pacific built west from the Missouri River at Omaha.

blocks.html: The first transcontinental railroad was finished at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. Congress paid for much of it with land grants and government bonds (loans) in the Pacific Railway Act of 1862.

A railroad across 1,900 miles of plains, deserts and mountains cost far more than private investors would risk on empty land. During the war, Congress and President Lincoln wanted the West tied to the Union. So the Pacific Railway Act gave the two companies alternate square-mile sections of public land beside the track (a checkerboard they could sell to settlers) and loaned them government bonds for each mile built, more per mile in the mountains. Later railroads across the North and South got land grants too.

The work was hard and dangerous. The Central Pacific hired thousands of Chinese workers, who by the peak made up most of its crews; they blasted tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada. The Union Pacific relied heavily on Irish immigrants and Civil War veterans. Chinese workers were paid less than white workers and were left out of the famous photographs of the final spike.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.q: A farmer in Kansas in 1880 can now sell wheat in Chicago and New York. Which change made that possible, and what did it lead to?
steps: The railroad carried heavy goods cheaply and quickly between the Plains and the cities.
Farmers could grow crops for distant markets, so more settlers came to the Plains.
More settlers and the railroads also brought hunters and soldiers onto Native lands, the subject of the next topic.
blocks.a: The railroad linked the Plains to national markets, which drew settlers and pushed Native nations off their lands.

blocks.html: Many people think private companies built the railroads on their own. They did the building, but Congress gave the Union Pacific and Central Pacific millions of acres of land and tens of millions of dollars in government bonds. The Crédit Mobilier scandal (exposed in 1872) showed how some Union Pacific insiders overcharged for construction and gave shares to members of Congress. Quick check: ask who paid. Both the companies and the public did.

The railroad also brought problems you will meet in this unit: the destruction of the bison, the conflicts on the Plains, the power of big railroad companies over farmers, and the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882.

blocks.html: The railroads brought settlers, miners and hunters onto the Great Plains. The Plains were not empty. They were the homelands of nations such as the Lakota (Sioux), Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche and Kiowa, many of whom lived by hunting the bison on horseback.

From the 1860s to 1890 the U.S. Army fought the Plains nations. Key events: the Sand Creek Massacre (1864), the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876), a Lakota and Cheyenne victory, and the killing of Lakota people at Wounded Knee (1890). By then most nations had been confined to reservations.

blocks.html: Three forces decided the outcome. First, the bison: herds of tens of millions were shot for hides and sport, with railroads carrying the hides east, until fewer than about 1,000 were left by 1889. Without the bison, the Plains nations lost their food, clothing and shelter. Second, disease and numbers: settlers kept coming, and the Army had railroads, supplies and reinforcements. Third, broken treaties: the Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868) promised the Black Hills to the Lakota, but after gold was found in 1874, miners poured in and the government tried to buy or take the land.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: The Little Bighorn (Montana) and Wounded Knee (South Dakota).

blocks.html: At Sand Creek in Colorado, on November 29, 1864, volunteer cavalry under Colonel John Chivington attacked a Cheyenne and Arapaho camp that believed it was under the Army's protection; most of those killed were women, children and older people. At the Little Bighorn in June 1876, Lakota and Cheyenne warriors led by Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Lieutenant Colonel George Custer's Seventh Cavalry. On December 29, 1890, at Wounded Knee in South Dakota, soldiers killed about 250 or more Lakota men, women and children (counts differ) during an attempt to disarm them, at a time of fear about the Ghost Dance movement.

blocks.title: Putting events in order
blocks.q: Order these: Wounded Knee; gold found in the Black Hills; the Treaty of Fort Laramie; the Little Bighorn.
steps: Treaty of Fort Laramie: 1868.
Gold found in the Black Hills: 1874.
Battle of the Little Bighorn: 1876.
Wounded Knee: 1890.
blocks.a: Fort Laramie, gold in the Black Hills, the Little Bighorn, Wounded Knee. The treaty came first, the gold broke it, and war followed.

blocks.html: Some students think the Plains nations simply lost every battle. They won some, the Little Bighorn most famously. What decided the outcome was the loss of the bison, disease, and the Army's numbers and supplies. Another slip: treating "the Indians" as one group. Each nation had its own leaders, alliances and rivalries.

blocks.html: After the wars on the Plains, federal policy changed from fighting Native nations to assimilation: trying to make Native people give up their languages, religions and ways of holding land and live like white American farmers. Reformers who backed it often said they were helping; the nations themselves lost children, culture and land.

Two tools of assimilation: boarding schools, such as the Carlisle Indian Industrial School (1879), and the Dawes Act (1887), which split land held in common by a tribe into family plots and sold the "surplus." Native landholding fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934.

Under the Dawes Act, also called the General Allotment Act, a head of family got a quarter section (160 acres) and a single adult an eighth (80 acres). The land was held in trust for 25 years, and those who took allotments could become citizens. Land left over after allotment could be sold to settlers. Many plots were poor for farming, families lacked tools and money, and after the trust ended much of the land was sold or lost. Land held together by a nation had been hard to buy; land held by individuals could be bought piece by piece.

paras: To each head of a family, one-quarter of a section; … To each single person over eighteen years of age, one-eighth of a section

marks.note: A section is one square mile (640 acres), so a quarter section is 160 acres.

blocks.html: At boarding schools such as Carlisle in Pennsylvania, founded by Richard Henry Pratt, children were often taken far from home, given new names and clothes, and punished for speaking their own languages. Pratt summed up his aim in 1892 as "Kill the Indian in him, and save the man." Many children died at the schools, far from their families. Some students later used their education to defend their nations.

blocks.title: Reading the numbers
blocks.q: Native landholding fell from about 138 million acres (1887) to about 48 million (1934). About what share was lost?
steps: Lost: 138 − 48 = 90 million acres.
Share lost: 90 ÷ 138 is about 0.65.
So about two-thirds of the land left Native hands in under 50 years.
blocks.a: About two-thirds.

blocks.html: Many students think the Dawes Act gave Native people more land. It broke up land held in common, and most of the land left Native hands. The policy of allotment ended with the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, which let nations rebuild their own governments.

blocks.html: The railroads were the first giant businesses, and they needed steel, coal and oil. In the decades after the Civil War the United States became the largest industrial economy in the world.

New industries (steel, oil, electricity, the telephone) and new ways of organizing business made a few firms enormous. They grew by vertical integration (owning every stage of making one product) and horizontal integration (buying or combining with competitors). The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) outlawed combinations "in restraint of trade."

blocks.html: Why did business grow so big so fast? Railroads made a national market. New technology, such as the Bessemer process, made steel cheap. Large firms could lower costs by producing more (economies of scale). Investors such as J. P. Morgan raised huge sums, and in 1901 Morgan bought Carnegie Steel to form U.S. Steel. Firms that controlled a market could also set prices, and that worried farmers, small businesses and many voters.

blocks.title: Which kind of growth?
blocks.q: A meatpacker buys cattle ranches, refrigerated railroad cars and butcher shops. Which kind of integration is this?
steps: Ask: are these competitors, or stages of one product?
Ranches (raw material), rail cars (transport), shops (sales) are stages of making and selling meat.
Owning the stages of one product is vertical integration.
blocks.a: Vertical integration.

blocks.html: Students often mix up vertical and horizontal integration. Vertical means owning each stage of making one product: think of a vertical chain from mine to mill to market. Horizontal means buying up competitors at the same stage: a horizontal row of rival firms. Note too that the Sherman Act was weak at first; in United States v. E. C. Knight Co. (1895) the Supreme Court held that manufacturing was not commerce.

People still argue about the leaders of this age. Some called them "robber barons" who crushed rivals and workers; others called them "captains of industry" who built the modern economy and gave fortunes to libraries and universities. Historians weigh both sides of the record.

blocks.html: The new industries needed millions of workers. Many worked ten to twelve hours a day, six days a week, in mills, mines and factories where injuries were common and there was no pay for those who were hurt. Children worked too. Workers formed unions to bargain together for better pay, shorter hours and safer work.

Two big national unions: the Knights of Labor (founded 1869; open to skilled and unskilled workers, including women and Black workers) and the American Federation of Labor (1886, led by Samuel Gompers; skilled craft unions focused on wages, hours and conditions). The Haymarket affair (1886), the Homestead strike (1892) and the Pullman strike (1894) turned violent and set unions back.

blocks.html: Why did strikes so often fail? Employers could hire replacement workers, and many new immigrants needed jobs. Most judges saw strikes as attacks on property and on trade, and issued injunctions (court orders) against them; the Pullman injunction even used the Sherman Antitrust Act against the union. Governors and Presidents sent militia and troops to keep trains and mills running. Violence, such as the Haymarket bomb, turned public opinion against unions, even when the unions had not caused it.

blocks.title: Comparing two unions
blocks.q: A skilled carpenter and an unskilled factory worker both want to join a union in 1888. Which union would take each?
steps: The AFL was a federation of craft unions for skilled workers.
The Knights of Labor took skilled and unskilled workers alike.
So the carpenter could join either; the unskilled worker would look to the Knights.
blocks.a: Carpenter: the AFL (or the Knights). Unskilled worker: the Knights of Labor.

blocks.html: Many students think the government usually sided with strikers. In the major strikes of this era, courts issued injunctions and state or federal troops were sent, mostly against the strikers. Government protection for unions came much later, with the Wagner Act of 1935.

blocks.html: The factories and mills drew workers from farms and from across the ocean. Cities grew fast: Chicago went from a small town in the 1840s to more than a million people by 1890.

From the 1880s, most immigrants came from southern and eastern Europe (Italy, Austria-Hungary, Russia and Greece), many through Ellis Island (opened 1892). Cities filled with crowded tenements, political machines such as Tammany Hall, and settlement houses such as Jane Addams's Hull House (1889). The Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) barred most Chinese laborers.

blocks.html: Why did they come? "Push" factors: poverty, crop failures, and in Russia attacks on Jewish communities. "Pull" factors: jobs in American industry, letters from relatives, cheap steamship tickets. In the cities, political machines traded help (jobs, coal in winter, help with the law) for votes, and leaders such as Boss Tweed of Tammany Hall stole public money. Settlement houses, run mostly by educated young women, offered English classes, child care and clubs, and pushed for better laws.

Many native-born Americans feared the newcomers would take jobs or change the culture; this nativism grew. On the West Coast, hostility toward Chinese workers led to the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, the first federal law to bar a group of immigrants by nationality. It was not repealed until 1943. Photographer Jacob Riis showed the crowded tenements in How the Other Half Lives (1890).

blocks.title: Push or pull?
blocks.q: Sort these reasons for an Italian farmer to leave for New York in 1900: poor harvests at home; a cousin's letter about jobs; high taxes; cheap steamship fares.
steps: Push factors drive people out of their home country: poor harvests, high taxes.
Pull factors draw them to the new one: the cousin's news of jobs.
Cheap fares made the trip possible; most historians count them as a pull.
blocks.a: Push: harvests, taxes. Pull: the letter about jobs, cheap fares.

blocks.html: A popular story says Ellis Island officials changed immigrants' names. Passenger lists were made at the port of departure, and inspectors checked names against them. Most name changes came later, made by the immigrants themselves, often to sound more American at work or school.

blocks.html: Mark Twain called this period the Gilded Age: shiny gold on the outside, cheaper metal underneath. Elections were close, turnout was high, and the two parties were evenly matched. Meanwhile machines in the cities and big companies held great power.

Reforms of the era: the Pendleton Act (1883) began a merit-based civil service after President Garfield's assassination; the Interstate Commerce Act (1887) set up the first federal regulatory commission, for railroads. Struggling farmers formed the People's (Populist) Party (1892). In 1896 William McKinley (gold standard) defeated William Jennings Bryan (free silver).

Under the spoils system, winners gave government jobs to supporters. In 1881 a disappointed office seeker shot President James Garfield, and Congress answered with the Pendleton Act: some federal jobs would go to people who passed exams. On the farms, prices for crops fell for decades while railroad rates and debts stayed high. Farmers organized in the Grange and the Farmers' Alliances, and in 1892 the Populists' Omaha Platform called for free coinage of silver, a graduated income tax, the direct election of senators, and government ownership of the railroads.

blocks.title: Who wanted what?
blocks.q: A Kansas farmer owes the bank \$1,000. Why would he want more silver coined, and why would the banker disagree?
steps: More money in circulation tends to raise prices, including crop prices.
Higher crop prices make a fixed debt of \$1,000 easier to repay.
The banker who lent the money wants to be paid in dollars that hold their value, so he favors gold.
blocks.a: Debtors wanted more money (silver, higher prices); creditors wanted sound money (gold).

blocks.html: The free-silver debate was not about jewelry or coins for their own sake. It was about the money supply: farmers in debt wanted more money in circulation and higher prices, while bankers and creditors favored the gold standard. After 1896 new gold discoveries raised the money supply anyway, and the Gold Standard Act of 1900 settled the question for a time.

blocks.html: The Reconstruction Amendments promised equal protection and the vote. After Reconstruction ended, Southern states found ways around both. These laws and customs were called Jim Crow.

Southern states passed segregation laws and kept Black citizens from voting with poll taxes, literacy tests and grandfather clauses. In Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) the Supreme Court upheld "separate but equal," 7 to 1, over Justice John Marshall Harlan's dissent. Journalist Ida B. Wells campaigned against lynching.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.facts: Louisiana's Separate Car Act of 1890 required railroads to provide separate cars for Black and white passengers. Homer Plessy, who was one-eighth Black, sat in a whites-only car in a planned test case and was arrested.
opts.reasoning: Justice Henry Billings Brown wrote that the law was a reasonable use of state power and that separation did not by itself mark anyone as inferior.
opts.dissent: Justice Harlan: the Constitution recognizes no classes among citizens, and the law was meant to keep Black citizens apart, not to treat everyone equally.

blocks.cap: The case brief. Brown v. Board of Education overturned it for public schools in 1954.

doc.title: Justice Harlan's dissent in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
paras: Our constitution is color-blind, and neither knows nor tolerates classes among citizens.

marks.note: Harlan argued that the law must treat all citizens the same, whatever their race.

blocks.html: How did states keep people from voting without breaking the Fifteenth Amendment, which forbids denying the vote "on account of race"? They used rules that did not name race. A poll tax charged a fee to vote. A literacy test was judged by local officials, who passed white voters and failed Black ones. A grandfather clause excused men from these rules if their grandfathers could vote before 1867, which covered most white men and almost no Black men. The Supreme Court struck down grandfather clauses in 1915, but poll taxes and tests lasted until the 1960s.

Violence enforced the system. Thousands of Black Americans were lynched, killed by mobs without trial, between the 1880s and the 1960s. After three Black grocers were lynched in Memphis in 1892, Ida B. Wells investigated lynchings across the South and published her findings in Southern Horrors (1892), showing that the usual excuses were often false.

blocks.title: Name the device
blocks.q: A county clerk asks a Black man to explain a clause of the state constitution and fails him, but lets white men register without the test. What device is this, and which amendment was it meant to get around?
steps: A test of reading or understanding before registering is a literacy test.
It was applied unequally by the clerk.
It avoided naming race, to get around the Fifteenth Amendment.
blocks.a: A literacy test, used to get around the Fifteenth Amendment.

blocks.html: Many students think separate facilities were in fact equal under Plessy. The schools, cars and waiting rooms provided for Black citizens were almost always worse, and courts rarely checked. The doctrine stood until Brown v. Board of Education (1954) overturned it for public schools.

blocks.html: The new fortunes and the new poverty of the industrial age raised hard questions. Is great wealth earned? What do the rich owe others? And after Jim Crow, how should Black Americans win their rights? Thinkers gave very different answers.

Four answers about wealth and society: Carnegie's "Gospel of Wealth" (the rich should give their fortunes away wisely), Social Darwinism (competition sorts the fit from the unfit, so government should not interfere), the Social Gospel (faith calls Christians to reform society) and reformers' plans such as Henry George's single tax. Two strategies for Black advancement: Booker T. Washington (skills and economic progress first) and W. E. B. Du Bois (full rights and higher education now).

blocks.html: These ideas mattered because they shaped what people thought government should do. If competition was natural law, then laws limiting hours or breaking up trusts were mistakes. If society made poverty, then reform was a duty. Washington and Du Bois both wanted Black Americans to rise; they disagreed about the order and the means. Washington built Tuskegee Institute and won support from white business leaders; Du Bois helped found the Niagara Movement (1905) and the NAACP (1909).

They shared the goal of Black progress but split over strategy: Washington stressed vocational education and economic progress first and did not openly challenge segregation; Du Bois demanded full civil and political rights and higher education now. blocks.html: By the 1890s the frontier was settled, factories made more than Americans could buy, and other powers were taking colonies around the world. Many leaders argued the United States needed overseas markets, naval bases and a strong navy. Others, remembering the ideals of the age's debates and of the Declaration, thought ruling other peoples went against American principles.

In 1893 American planters and businessmen in Hawaii, backed by U.S. Marines, overthrew Queen Liliuokalani; the U.S. annexed Hawaii in 1898. The Spanish-American War (1898) brought Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines, where a long war against Filipino independence fighters followed (1899 to 1902).

blocks.html: Why war with Spain? Cubans had risen against Spanish rule. American newspapers owned by William Randolph Hearst and Joseph Pulitzer printed sensational stories of Spanish cruelty ("yellow journalism"), and Americans had money in Cuban sugar. When the battleship USS Maine exploded in Havana harbor in February 1898, many blamed Spain (the cause is still debated; one later study pointed to an accident). Congress declared war in April, promising in the Teller Amendment not to annex Cuba. The war lasted under four months. Commodore George Dewey destroyed Spain's fleet at Manila Bay, and the Rough Riders and Black regiments fought at San Juan Hill.

blocks.cap: Hawaii (1898) joined the earlier acquisitions. The simplified map does not show Puerto Rico, Guam or the Philippines.

blocks.html: In the Treaty of Paris (1898), Spain freed Cuba, ceded Puerto Rico and Guam, and sold the Philippines for \$20 million. Filipinos led by Emilio Aguinaldo had expected independence and fought the Americans from 1899. More than 4,200 American soldiers died, more than 20,000 Filipino fighters were killed, and as many as 200,000 Filipino civilians died of violence, famine and disease. Cuba became independent, but the Platt Amendment (1901) let the U.S. intervene there and keep a naval base at Guantánamo Bay.

blocks.title: Weighing the debate
blocks.q: In 1899 the Senate debated the treaty. Give one argument from each side.
steps: For empire: markets for American goods, coaling stations for the navy, rivalry with other powers, and a claimed duty to "civilize" (a view many then held and many now reject).

Against: the Anti-Imperialist League (Mark Twain, Andrew Carnegie and others) said ruling people without their consent broke the principle of the Declaration; some also feared competition or new citizens.
The Senate ratified the treaty in February 1899, by one vote more than the two-thirds needed.
blocks.a: Supporters stressed trade, power and a mission abroad; opponents stressed consent of the governed.

blocks.html: Many students think the war with Spain was fought only in Cuba. It began over Cuba, but American forces also fought in the Philippines (Manila Bay) and took Puerto Rico and Guam. Another slip: thinking the war ended American fighting there. The war against Filipino independence fighters lasted longer and cost far more lives than the war with Spain.

blocks.html: After the war with Spain, the United States had interests across the Pacific and the Caribbean. Three presidents in a row shaped how it used its new power, each with a slogan.

The Open Door notes (1899) asked equal trading rights for all in China. Theodore Roosevelt backed Panama's independence (1903) and built the Panama Canal (opened 1914), and added the Roosevelt Corollary (1904) to the Monroe Doctrine. William Howard Taft favored dollar diplomacy. Woodrow Wilson spoke of moral diplomacy but also sent troops to the Caribbean and Mexico.

blocks.html: Why a canal? Ships sailing from New York to San Francisco had to go around South America. When Colombia's senate refused Roosevelt's treaty terms, Panamanian rebels declared independence in November 1903 with U.S. warships nearby; the new nation quickly signed a treaty giving the U.S. a canal zone. Building the canal took ten years and more than 5,000 workers' lives, many from disease. The Roosevelt Corollary said that if a Latin American country could not pay its debts or keep order, the United States, not European powers, would step in. The Monroe Doctrine had warned Europe away; the Corollary claimed a right for the U.S. to intervene.

blocks.html: The growing cities and giant companies had real problems: slums, child labor, unsafe factories, impure food, corrupt city governments. Around 1900 a new kind of journalist set out to expose them, and readers of cheap new magazines such as McClure's paid attention.

Muckrakers exposed problems: Jacob Riis (city slums, 1890), Ida Tarbell (Standard Oil, 1904), Lincoln Steffens (city corruption), Upton Sinclair (The Jungle, meatpacking, 1906). In 1906 Congress passed the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act.

Immigrant workers' lives and filthy conditions in Chicago meatpacking

blocks.html: The name came from Theodore Roosevelt, who in 1906 compared reporters who saw only filth to a man in an old story who raked muck instead of looking up. He meant it partly as a warning, but the writers took the name with pride. Their work fed a broad Progressive movement of reformers, many of them middle-class, who believed experts, facts and government action could fix the problems of industrial life. After the Triangle Shirtwaist fire in New York killed 146 garment workers in 1911 (one of the exit doors had been locked), New York passed dozens of factory safety laws.

Sinclair, a socialist, wanted readers to care about the workers. Readers were most upset about what went into their sausages. Sales of meat fell, President Roosevelt sent inspectors, and within months Congress passed both 1906 laws. Sinclair later wrote, "I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach."

blocks.title: From exposé to law
blocks.q: Trace the chain from The Jungle to the new laws.
steps: 1906: The Jungle describes the meatpacking plants.
Readers are outraged about food safety; meat sales fall.
Roosevelt orders an investigation, which confirms much of it.
June 30, 1906: the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act are signed.
blocks.a: Exposé, public outrage, investigation, law: the Progressive pattern.

blocks.html: Many students think Sinclair wrote The Jungle to expose unsafe food. He meant to show the hard lives of immigrant workers and to argue for socialism; readers reacted most to the meat. A second slip: muckrakers held no office. They were writers whose facts pushed officials to act.

blocks.html: The muckrakers showed the problems; Progressive presidents used federal power to address them. Three presidents in a row, two Republicans and a Democrat, called themselves Progressives, though they disagreed about how far to go.

Theodore Roosevelt (1901–1909) sued trusts, regulated railroads and food, and protected about 230 million acres of public land. Taft (1909–1913) filed even more antitrust suits; Standard Oil was broken up in 1911. Woodrow Wilson (1913–1921) signed the Federal Reserve Act (1913) and, in 1914, the Clayton Antitrust Act and the Federal Trade Commission Act.

head: President
Name for his program
Main acts
rows: Northern Securities suit (won 1904); settled the 1902 coal strike; Hepburn Act (1906); food and drug laws (1906); 150 national forests
About 90 antitrust suits; Standard Oil and American Tobacco broken up (1911); proposed the income tax amendment
Lower tariffs and an income tax (1913); Federal Reserve (1913); Clayton Act and FTC (1914); child labor law (1916)

blocks.html: The election of 1912 shows the debate. Roosevelt, angry that Taft had broken with his allies, ran on a new Progressive ("Bull Moose") ticket for a New Nationalism: accept big business, but regulate it with a strong federal government. Wilson's New Freedom aimed to break up monopolies and restore competition among smaller firms. With the Republicans split, Wilson won 435 electoral votes to Roosevelt's 88 and Taft's 8; the Socialist Eugene Debs won about 6 percent of the popular vote. In office, Wilson ended up creating new regulators too. The Progressive era had limits: Wilson's administration also segregated several federal departments.

blocks.title: Good trust or bad trust?
blocks.q: Roosevelt said he did not oppose bigness itself. How would he treat a huge firm that cut prices and treated customers fairly, versus a railroad combination that fixed rates?
steps: Roosevelt sorted trusts by conduct, not size.
A large firm acting fairly: regulate and watch it.
A combination that crushed competition and fixed rates: sue to break it up, as with Northern Securities.
blocks.a: Regulate the "good" trust; break up the "bad" one.

blocks.html: Many students think Roosevelt opposed all big business. He distinguished "good" trusts from "bad" ones and preferred regulating most large companies to breaking them up. In fact Taft filed more antitrust suits (about 90) than Roosevelt (44).

blocks.html: Progressives also changed the rules of government itself. Some reforms needed only state laws; others needed amendments to the Constitution, which had not been amended since 1870.

Four amendments in seven years: the Sixteenth (federal income tax, 1913), Seventeenth (senators elected by the voters, 1913), Eighteenth (Prohibition, 1919) and Nineteenth (women's suffrage, 1920). Many states also adopted the initiative, referendum, recall and direct primary.

blocks.name: cv-amend
blocks.cap: The 27 amendments by year. The four Progressive amendments came after a gap of 43 years.

head: Reform
What it lets voters do
Early example
rows: Propose a law by petition and vote on it
Vote on a law the legislature passed
Remove an official before the term ends, by petition and vote
Choose party nominees by vote instead of by party bosses

blocks.html: Why these changes? Progressives believed bosses, machines and big money stood between the people and their government. State legislatures that chose senators were often bribed or deadlocked, so the Seventeenth Amendment gave the choice to the voters. The Supreme Court had struck down a federal income tax in 1895, so the Sixteenth Amendment allowed one without dividing it among the states by population. Reformers saw drinking as a cause of poverty and family violence, so the Eighteenth Amendment banned making, selling and transporting alcohol. Women argued that voting was their right and that they would help clean up politics.

blocks.title: Which tool?
blocks.q: Voters in a state collect signatures to put a new minimum-wage law on the ballot and pass it themselves. Which reform did they use?
steps: They did not vote on a law the legislature passed (that is a referendum).
They did not remove an official (recall).
Proposing and passing their own law by petition is the initiative.
blocks.a: The initiative.

blocks.html: Many students think senators were always elected by voters. Under the original Constitution (Article I, Section 3), state legislatures chose senators. The Seventeenth Amendment (1913) changed that. Another mix-up: Prohibition was the Eighteenth Amendment and was repealed by the Twenty-first (1933); it is the only amendment ever repealed.

blocks.html: The fight for women's right to vote began long before the Progressive Era, at Seneca Falls in 1848. It took 72 years, two generations of leaders and two very different strategies to win the Nineteenth Amendment.

After decades of work by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony and others, Carrie Chapman Catt's National American Woman Suffrage Association lobbied state by state, while Alice Paul's National Woman's Party picketed the White House. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified on August 18, 1920, when Tennessee became the 36th state to approve it.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: States where women had full voting rights before the Nineteenth Amendment (highlighted), most of them in the West. Wyoming was first, as a territory in 1869.

blocks.html: Why did the West lead? New territories wanted settlers and families, women's work on farms and ranches was plainly essential, and Western politics were less fixed. Wyoming (1869 as a territory), Colorado (1893), Utah and Idaho (1896) came first; Washington (1910) and California (1911) started a second wave. Each state victory added voters whom members of Congress had to answer to. During World War I, suffragists pointed out that women were serving the war effort while the country fought "for democracy" abroad. In 1918 President Wilson came out for the amendment, and Congress passed it in June 1919.

head: NAWSA (Catt)
National Woman's Party (Paul)
rows: About two million; the larger group
"Winning Plan" (1916): win states, then press Congress; lobby politely; support the war effort
Parades (1913), picketing the White House as "Silent Sentinels" (from 1917), hunger strikes in jail
blocks.cap: Two strategies, one goal. Historians generally say both pressures mattered.

blocks.title: Counting to ratification
blocks.q: In 1920 there were 48 states. How many had to ratify the amendment?
steps: Article V requires three-fourths of the states.
Three-fourths of 48 is 36.
Tennessee was the 36th, on August 18, 1920, when the young legislator Harry Burn changed his vote after a letter from his mother.
blocks.a: 36 states.

blocks.html: Many students think no woman voted anywhere before 1920. Wyoming let women vote from 1869, and by 1919 women had full voting rights in fifteen states, most in the West, and could vote for President in several more. The opposite slip matters too: the amendment did not end every barrier. Many Black women in the South were still kept from voting by Jim Crow laws, and many Native women could not vote until later.

blocks.html: Under Jim Crow, Black Southerners faced segregation, the loss of the vote, lynching and sharecropping debts. In the early 1900s they answered in two great ways: by organizing, and by leaving.

The NAACP (founded 1909) fought segregation and lynching in the courts and in public. From about 1910 to 1970, roughly six million Black Southerners moved to cities of the North and West in the Great Migration, for jobs and to escape Jim Crow.

events.label: The Crisis begins (editor W. E. B. Du Bois)
Guinn v. United States strikes down grandfather clauses
U.S. enters World War I; factory jobs open

Second, larger wave begins with World War II

blocks.html: Why move? Push factors: Jim Crow, violence, low pay, and the boll weevil, which wrecked cotton crops in the 1910s. Pull factors: when World War I cut off immigration from Europe and factories needed workers, Northern employers recruited in the South. Newspapers such as the Chicago Defender printed job ads and letters from those who had gone. Migrants found higher wages and the vote, but also crowded housing, segregated neighborhoods and, in 1919, deadly riots in Chicago and other cities.

The NAACP was founded in 1909 by a group of Black and white reformers, including W. E. B. Du Bois, Ida B. Wells and Mary White Ovington, after a race riot in Springfield, Illinois. Du Bois edited its magazine, The Crisis. Its lawyers won early cases against grandfather clauses (1915) and residential segregation laws (1917), building toward Brown v. Board of Education.

blocks.name: cv-map
blocks.cap: Migrants went from the South to cities such as Chicago, Detroit, New York and, in the second wave, Los Angeles.

blocks.title: Reading a cause
blocks.q: Why did the first big wave of the Great Migration start around 1916 rather than 1900?
steps: Jim Crow existed in 1900 too, so it cannot explain the timing alone.
In 1914 to 1918 the war cut immigration from Europe while war factories needed workers.
The new jobs (a pull) added to the old pushes and set off the wave.
blocks.a: War jobs and the drop in European immigration created a new pull.

blocks.html: Many students think the Great Migration happened all at once. It came in two big waves, around the two World Wars, over six decades: about 1.6 million people from 1910 to 1940, and about five million more from 1940 to 1970.

blocks.html: When war broke out in Europe in the summer of 1914, between the Allies (Britain, France, Russia) and the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire), most Americans wanted no part of it. The country had just flexed its power in its own hemisphere, but Europe's war seemed far away.

The U.S. stayed neutral from 1914. German submarine attacks (the Lusitania, 1915; unrestricted submarine warfare, from February 1917) and the Zimmermann Telegram (made public March 1917) led Congress to declare war on Germany on April 6, 1917.

blocks.name: cv-timeline

events.label: War begins in Europe; U.S. declares neutrality
Wilson reelected: "He kept us out of war"

blocks.cap: Neutral for two and a half years, then war in 1917.

blocks.html: Neutral did not mean untouched. Britain blockaded Germany, so American trade and loans flowed mostly to the Allies. Germany answered with submarines (U-boats), which sank ships without warning. After the Lusitania went down in May 1915, killing 1,198 people including 128 Americans, Wilson protested, and in 1916 Germany promised to limit its attacks. In January 1917 Germany decided to sink all ships near Britain anyway, gambling it could win before American troops arrived. Then the British decoded a telegram from Germany's foreign secretary, Arthur Zimmermann, offering Mexico an alliance.

doc.title: The Zimmermann Telegram (January 1917), as decoded
doc.source: Arthur Zimmermann to the German minister in Mexico (public domain translation)
paras: We intend to begin on the first of February unrestricted submarine warfare. We shall endeavor in spite of this to keep the United States of America neutral. In the event of this not succeeding, we make Mexico a proposal of alliance

marks.note: Sinking ships without warning, including neutral ones.
Germany offered to help Mexico recover land lost to the U.S. in the 1840s.

blocks.html: On April 2, 1917, Wilson asked Congress for war, saying the world must be made "safe for democracy." The Senate voted 82 to 6 and the House 373 to 50; Jeannette Rankin, the first woman in Congress, voted no.

blocks.title: Long-term and immediate causes
blocks.q: Sort these: American trade with the Allies; the Lusitania; unrestricted submarine warfare in 1917; the Zimmermann Telegram.
steps: Long-term: trade and loans tied the U.S. economy to the Allies (1914 to 1917).
Background: the Lusitania (1915) turned opinion against Germany but did not bring war.
Immediate: unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram (early 1917).
blocks.a: Trade and the Lusitania were background; the 1917 U-boat campaign and the telegram were the immediate causes.

blocks.html: Many students think the Lusitania sinking brought the U.S. into the war right away. It came almost two years before the U.S. entered. The renewed submarine campaign and the Zimmermann Telegram in early 1917 were the immediate causes.

blocks.html: Once Congress declared war, the federal government grew faster than ever before. It raised an army, ran the economy and worked to shape opinion. Then Wilson tried to shape the peace.

The government drafted soldiers (Selective Service Act, 1917), ran wartime agencies and limited dissent (the Espionage Act, 1917; Schenck v. United States, 1919). The war ended with the armistice of November 11, 1918. Wilson's Fourteen Points and League of Nations failed to win the Senate's approval of the Treaty of Versailles.

About 24 million men registered for the draft and 2.8 million were drafted; some two million soldiers went to France under General John J. Pershing. The War Industries Board directed factories, the Food Administration under Herbert Hoover urged "meatless" days, and the Committee on Public Information made posters and films for the war. Critics were prosecuted: Socialist leader Eugene Debs got ten years in prison for a speech. In Schenck the Supreme Court, 9 to 0, upheld a conviction for urging men to resist the draft; Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes wrote that speech could be punished when it creates a "clear and present danger."

doc.title: Schenck v. United States (1919), opinion of Justice Holmes
paras: The most stringent protection of free speech would not protect a man in falsely shouting fire in a theatre and causing a panic.

The question in every case is whether the words used are used in such circumstances and are of such a nature as to create a clear and present danger that they will bring about the substantive evils that Congress has a right to prevent.

marks.note: The test of the case. In 1969 the Court replaced it with a narrower test (Brandenburg v. Ohio).

blocks.html: Wilson's Fourteen Points (January 1918) called for open treaties, freedom of the seas, lower trade barriers, self-determination for peoples, and, in Point 14, "a general association of nations." At Paris in 1919 the Allies wrote a harsher treaty, but it included the League. In the Senate, Henry Cabot Lodge and his allies demanded reservations, especially to Article 10, which they feared could commit the U.S. to war without Congress. Wilson refused to compromise, then suffered a stroke. The Senate rejected the treaty in 1919 and again in 1920.

blocks.title: Why no League?
blocks.q: Wilson proposed the League. Why did the United States never join?
steps: The Constitution requires two-thirds of the Senate to approve a treaty.
Lodge's Republicans would approve only with reservations; a smaller group opposed the League entirely.
Wilson told Democrats to vote against the treaty with reservations, so neither version reached two-thirds.
blocks.a: The Senate never gave the two-thirds approval, so the U.S. stayed out.

blocks.html: Many students think the U.S. joined the League of Nations because Wilson proposed it. The Senate did not ratify the Treaty of Versailles, so the U.S. never joined. It made a separate peace with Germany in 1921.

events.label: Schenck v. United States; Treaty of Versailles signed

blocks.html: After the Great War and a short, sharp slump in 1920 and 1921, the economy boomed. Cities grew, and for the first time more Americans lived in urban areas than rural ones (the 1920 census). A new way of life, built on cars, radios, movies and buying on credit, spread across the country. Many of the migrants from the South helped make the new culture.

Cars (the Model T), radio, movies and installment buying created a mass consumer culture. Jazz spread from New Orleans to Chicago and New York, and the Harlem Renaissance (Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, Duke Ellington) flourished. But the prosperity was uneven: farmers struggled all decade.

head: Change
Example
Effect
rows: Ford's Model T (1908 to 1927), made on a moving assembly line from 1913; over 15 million built
Suburbs, roads, gas stations, motels; car makers became the biggest industry
KDKA in Pittsburgh began regular broadcasts in 1920
The same news, music and ads reached the whole country at once
The first feature film with spoken dialogue, The Jazz Singer (1927)
Shared stars and styles; millions went every week
"Buy now, pay later": installment plans for cars, radios and appliances
More spending, but also more household debt

blocks.html: Why did the decade "roar"? Factories that had made war goods switched to consumer goods. Electricity reached most city homes, so families bought refrigerators, washing machines and vacuum cleaners. Advertising, a growing industry, taught people to want new things, and credit let them buy before they had the money. Young women called flappers cut their hair short and wore shorter skirts; many women, newly able to vote, took jobs in offices and stores.

In Harlem, a neighborhood of New York, Black writers, artists and musicians created a burst of work now called the Harlem Renaissance. Langston Hughes wrote poems in the rhythms of jazz and blues; Zora Neale Hurston collected folklore and wrote novels; Duke Ellington led his orchestra at the Cotton Club; Louis Armstrong carried jazz from New Orleans to Chicago and beyond. Marcus Garvey's Universal Negro Improvement Association drew hundreds of thousands with a message of Black pride and self-reliance.

events.label: The Jazz Singer; Lindbergh flies the Atlantic

blocks.title: Who was left out?
blocks.q: A historian says, "The twenties were prosperous." What evidence would complicate that claim?
steps: Farm prices fell after the war, when Europe's farms recovered, and stayed low; many farmers lost their land.
Wealth and income grew fastest at the top; wages in coal and textiles lagged.
Many families bought on credit, so spending rested partly on debt.
blocks.a: Farmers, workers in "sick" industries and much of the rural South did not share the boom.

blocks.html: Many students think everyone prospered in the 1920s. Farmers struggled all decade, and wealth grew most at the top. The boom was real for millions of city families, but it was uneven, and that unevenness is one of the causes historians weigh for the Depression.

sources.name: OpenStax, U.S. History, Chapter 24, "The Jazz Age: Redefining the Nation, 1919–1929" (cited by book and chapter)

blocks.html: The new culture of the 1920s thrilled some Americans and alarmed others. Many in small towns and rural areas felt their values and way of life were under attack from cities, immigrants and new ideas. The conflicts of the decade show a country divided over change.

Conflicts of the twenties: the Red Scare (1919 to 1920), the Sacco and Vanzetti case, immigration quotas (1921, 1924), the Scopes trial (1925), a revived Ku Klux Klan, and the struggle to enforce Prohibition.

head: Conflict
What happened
rows: After the Russian Revolution, strikes and anarchist bombings in 1919, Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer's raids arrested thousands of suspected radicals; hundreds of immigrants were deported

Two Italian-born anarchists were convicted of a 1920 robbery and murder and executed in 1927; many believed their trial was unfair because of their politics and origins, and historians still debate their guilt
The Emergency Quota Act (1921) and the Immigration Act of 1924 limited immigration by national origin, favoring northern and western Europe; the 1924 act barred most immigration from Asia

In Dayton, Tennessee, teacher John Scopes was tried for teaching evolution; William Jennings Bryan helped prosecute and Clarence Darrow defended; Scopes was convicted and fined, a verdict later overturned on a technicality
Revived in 1915, it claimed millions of members in the mid-1920s, in the North and West as well as the South, targeting Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants, until scandals shrank it

blocks.html: What tied these together? Rapid change: cities, new immigrants, science, women's new roles, and fears of revolution after 1917. Some answered with laws (quotas, Prohibition, the Tennessee law against teaching evolution); some with fear of outsiders; some with violence. Defenders of the quota laws argued they protected American workers and culture; critics, then and now, saw them as discrimination by national origin. The quotas lasted until 1965.

doc.title: The Eighteenth Amendment (1919), Section 1
paras: the manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors within, the importation thereof into, or the exportation thereof from the United States and all territory subject to the jurisdiction thereof for beverage purposes is hereby prohibited.

marks.note: What the amendment banned. It did not ban drinking itself.

blocks.title: Reading the amendment closely
blocks.q: Under Prohibition, was it a federal crime to drink a glass of wine at home?
steps: Read the verbs: "manufacture, sale, or transportation," plus import and export.
Drinking is not on the list.
So making, selling or moving alcohol was banned, while drinking alcohol already owned was not.
blocks.a: No. The amendment and the Volstead Act banned making, selling and moving alcohol, not drinking it.

blocks.html: Many students think Prohibition banned drinking alcohol. The Eighteenth Amendment banned making, selling and transporting it. Enforcement was hard: speakeasies and bootleggers thrived, and gangsters such as Al Capone grew rich. It was repealed by the Twenty-first Amendment in 1933.

blocks.html: Through the late 1920s, stock prices climbed. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose from 63 in August 1921 to 381 in September 1929. Millions of Americans bought stock, many with borrowed money. Then in the autumn of 1929 prices fell, and kept falling.

Stocks crashed in October 1929 (Black Tuesday, October 29). The Great Depression followed: by 1933 about a quarter of workers were jobless. Historians and economists weigh several causes: speculation and buying on margin, bank failures, a shrinking money supply, overproduction and weak demand, unequal income, and high tariffs.

Buying on margin meant paying as little as 10 percent of a stock's price and borrowing the rest. When prices fell, brokers demanded repayment, forcing investors to sell, which pushed prices lower. The crash wiped out savings and confidence. But a crash alone need not cause a decade-long depression. What turned a downturn into the Great Depression? That is where economists disagree about the weights.

head: Cause
The argument
Who stresses it
rows: Bank failures and the money supply
More than 9,000 banks failed from 1930 to 1933; the money supply fell by about a third, and the Federal Reserve did not stop it
Monetarist economists (Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz)
Spending by consumers and businesses collapsed, and nothing replaced it
Factories and farms made more than people with modest incomes could buy; much of the gain of the 1920s went to the top
The Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) raised duties; other nations retaliated and world trade shrank
Most economists count it as a cause, though they debate how large
Easy credit fed a bubble; the crash destroyed wealth and confidence
blocks.cap: Several causes, weighed differently.

events.label: Smoot-Hawley Tariff; first wave of bank panics

blocks.title: How margin magnifies a fall
blocks.q: An investor buys \$1,000 of stock with \$100 of her own money and \$900 borrowed. The stock falls 20 percent. What happens?
steps: The stock is now worth 0.8 × 1,000 = 800 dollars.
She still owes the broker 900 dollars.
Her 100 dollars is gone, and she owes 100 dollars more: a 20 percent fall cost her more than everything she put in.
blocks.a: She loses her whole stake and still owes money, so she must sell, which pushes prices lower.

blocks.html: Many students think the Crash alone caused the Great Depression. Most economists see the Crash as one cause among several, and they debate how much weight to give each. A sign that it was not the whole story: stocks had recovered a little by spring 1930, before the bank panics that followed.

blocks.html: The Crash was followed by three years of decline. Factories closed, farms were lost, and banks failed, taking families' savings with them. There was no federal deposit insurance and, for most workers, no unemployment insurance.

By 1933 about a quarter of workers were unemployed; thousands of banks failed; drought and dust storms drove families from the Plains (the Dust Bowl). Herbert Hoover's Reconstruction Finance Corporation (1932) lent to banks and businesses, and the Bonus Army was driven from Washington (1932).

Life changed for almost everyone. Families doubled up in apartments, delayed marriage and children, and stood in bread lines. Shantytowns of the homeless were called Hoovervilles. On the southern Plains, years of plowing up grasslands followed by drought let the wind strip the soil; on "Black Sunday," April 14, 1935, a vast dust storm turned day into night. Hundreds of thousands of people, many from Oklahoma, moved west to California looking for work. Between about 400,000 and a million people of Mexican descent, many of them U.S. citizens, left or were pushed out of the country in "repatriation" drives.

head: Hoover did
Hoover would not
rows: Asked business leaders to keep wages up (1929)
Give federal money directly to the unemployed
Expanded public works, including the dam later named for him
Run a large budget deficit for long
Created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation (January 1932) to lend to banks, railroads and businesses
Accept that charity and local government could not meet the need
Signed the Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930), now widely blamed for shrinking trade
blocks.cap: Hoover believed direct federal relief would weaken self-reliance ("rugged individualism").

blocks.html: In the summer of 1932, thousands of World War I veterans and their families, the Bonus Army, camped in Washington to ask for early payment of a bonus promised for 1945. Congress refused. On July 28, after a clash with police, Army troops under General Douglas MacArthur drove the veterans out and burned their camp. The scene hurt Hoover badly in the election that fall.

blocks.title: Judging a record fairly
blocks.q: A student writes, "Hoover did nothing about the Depression." Correct the claim using evidence.
steps: Hoover did more than earlier presidents in downturns: public works and the RFC (1932).
But he opposed direct federal relief to individuals and hoped confidence and voluntary action would bring recovery.
So the fair claim: he acted, but within limits, and the slump deepened.
blocks.a: Hoover acted (public works, the RFC) but refused direct federal relief.

blocks.html: Many students think Hoover did nothing. He did more than earlier presidents in downturns (public works, the RFC) but opposed direct federal relief to individuals. Another slip: the Dust Bowl was not caused by the Crash. It came from drought and farming practices on the southern Plains.

blocks.html: In 1932 voters chose Franklin D. Roosevelt over Hoover. By his inauguration on March 4, 1933, banks in most states had closed. Roosevelt promised action: "the only thing we have to fear is fear itself." In his first Hundred Days, Congress passed fifteen major laws.

The New Deal aimed at relief, recovery and reform. Key programs: the CCC and TVA (1933), deposit insurance (FDIC, 1933), the SEC (1934), the WPA, Social Security and the Wagner Act (1935), and the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938).

doc.title: Franklin D. Roosevelt, First Inaugural Address (March 4, 1933)
paras: So, first of all, let me assert my firm belief that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself—nameless, unreasoning, unjustified terror which paralyzes needed efforts to convert retreat into advance.

marks.note: Roosevelt blamed panic, such as runs on banks, for making the crisis worse.

Year
What it did
R

Dams, flood control and electric power for a poor region
Insured bank deposits, ending bank runs
Millions of jobs building roads, schools and post offices, and for artists and writers
Old-age pensions and unemployment insurance, paid for by payroll taxes
Protected workers' right to form unions and bargain
A minimum wage (25 cents an hour at first), limits on hours, an end to most child labor

blocks.html: Why such a mix? Roosevelt was willing to experiment and to drop what failed. The first New Deal (1933 to 1934) tried to stop the collapse and plan recovery with business and farmers. The second New Deal (1935 to 1936) built lasting safety nets and protections for workers. Frances Perkins, his labor secretary and the first woman in a cabinet, shaped Social Security and the labor laws.

blocks.title: Sort by the three Rs
blocks.q: Is each relief, recovery or reform: WPA jobs; the SEC; the TVA?
steps: Relief helps people now: a WPA paycheck.
Recovery aims to restart the economy: the TVA's dams and power for a region.
Reform aims to prevent another crash: the SEC policing the stock market.
blocks.a: WPA: relief. TVA: recovery. SEC: reform.

blocks.html: Students mix up the three Rs. Relief helped people now (WPA jobs, the CCC). Recovery aimed to restart the economy (the TVA, the farm and industry programs). Reform aimed to prevent another crash and protect people for good (the FDIC, the SEC, Social Security). Some programs did more than one.

blocks.html: The New Deal stretched federal power further than ever in peacetime. Its laws reached factories, farms and wages, which the Supreme Court had long treated as matters for the states. A clash between the President and the Court followed, a case study in checks and balances.

The Court struck down parts of the New Deal (Schechter, 1935). Roosevelt's 1937 plan to add justices failed in Congress, but that year the Court began upholding economic regulation (West Coast Hotel v. Parrish; NLRB v. Jones & Laughlin).

opts.facts: Under the National Industrial Recovery Act, codes written with industry groups set wages, hours and trade practices. The Schechter brothers, Brooklyn poultry dealers, were convicted of breaking the poultry code ("the sick chicken case").
opts.reasoning: Congress gave away lawmaking power to the President and industry groups, and the business was local, affecting interstate commerce only indirectly.

blocks.html: In 1935 and 1936 the Court struck down the National Industrial Recovery Act (Schechter) and the first farm program (United States v. Butler, 1936). After winning a landslide in 1936, Roosevelt proposed in February 1937 to add up to six new justices, one for each justice over 70 who did not retire. Critics, including many Democrats, called it "court packing" and an attack on judicial independence; the Senate set it aside that summer. Meanwhile, in March and April 1937, the Court upheld a state minimum wage (West Coast Hotel, 5 to 4) and the Wagner Act (Jones & Laughlin, 5 to 4), and in May it upheld Social Security.

opts.facts: Elsie Parrish, a hotel maid in Washington State, sued for back pay under the state's minimum wage law for women.
opts.reasoning: Liberty of contract is not absolute; a state may protect workers' health and bargaining position.

The Court's rulings shifted anyway (some point to Justice Owen Roberts's vote, which historians show was cast in West Coast Hotel before the plan was announced), and retirements soon let Roosevelt appoint new justices. The Court has had nine seats since 1869.

blocks.html: Was the New Deal a success? Americans argued about it fiercely at the time, from both sides, and historians and economists still debate it. A fair judgment starts with the evidence and with each side's strongest case.

Critics on the left (Huey Long, Father Coughlin, Francis Townsend) said the New Deal did too little; critics on the right (the American Liberty League) said it did too much. Scholars still debate how much it helped recovery, while agreeing it changed the federal government's role for good.

blocks.html: What does the evidence show? Unemployment fell from about 25 percent in 1933 to about 14 percent in 1937, then rose again to nearly 20 percent in the recession of 1937 to 1938, after spending was cut and the Federal Reserve tightened. It stayed above 14 percent through 1940. Some programs lasted and are now part of American life: Social Security, deposit insurance (the waves of bank runs of the early 1930s did not return), the SEC, the minimum wage. The New Deal also left out many: early Social Security excluded farm and household workers, and some programs were run in segregated ways.

Main argument
rows: The New Deal saved the system
It stopped the panic, restored banks, gave relief to millions and built lasting protections, preserving both democracy and capitalism
Spending was too small and too cautious to end the Depression; only wartime spending did (a Keynesian argument)
Price-fixing codes and uncertainty for business held back investment; monetary policy, such as leaving the gold standard, did more for recovery (argued by some economists)
blocks.cap: Present each with its evidence; scholars still weigh them.

blocks.a: Lasting programs and new expectations support the claim, whatever one thinks of the recovery record.

blocks.html: Students take one side's view as the agreed verdict. Present each view with its evidence: unemployment fell but stayed high until the war; programs such as Social Security and deposit insurance lasted. "Which is right" is the debate itself, not a settled fact.

blocks.html: While Americans fought the Depression, dictators rose abroad. Japan invaded Manchuria (1931) and China (1937); Italy invaded Ethiopia (1935); Nazi Germany rearmed and seized Austria and Czechoslovakia. Most Americans, remembering the Great War, wanted to stay out.

The Neutrality Acts (1935 to 1937) aimed to keep the U.S. out of foreign wars. After war began in Europe (1939), cash and carry, Lend-Lease (March 1941) and the Atlantic Charter (August 1941) moved the country toward the Allies, while isolationists argued against it.

blocks.html: Why neutrality laws? A Senate committee led by Gerald Nye (1934 to 1936) argued that bankers and arms makers had pulled the U.S. into World War I. The Neutrality Acts banned selling arms to nations at war and, later, travel on their ships. When Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939, Roosevelt got Congress to allow arms sales on a cash-and-carry basis: buyers paid cash and carried goods in their own ships, which favored Britain and France, who controlled the seas. After France fell in 1940, Britain stood almost alone. Roosevelt traded fifty old destroyers for bases, called the U.S. the "arsenal of democracy," and, when Britain ran out of cash, won Lend-Lease: weapons lent or leased to nations whose defense was vital to the U.S.

blocks.html: Through 1941, the United States moved step by step toward the Allies in Europe. In Asia, Japan was at war in China and pushing into Southeast Asia. In the summer of 1941 the U.S. froze Japanese assets and cut off oil sales. Japan's leaders decided to strike first.

On December 7, 1941, Japan attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii. Congress declared war on Japan the next day, December 8. Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on December 11.

doc.source: Public domain (a work of the U.S. government)

I ask that the Congress declare that since the unprovoked and dastardly attack by Japan on Sunday, December 7th, 1941, a state of war has existed between the United States and the Japanese Empire.

marks.note: Infamy: lasting shame. Roosevelt framed the attack as a betrayal, since talks were still going on.

blocks.html: Japan wanted to knock out the U.S. Pacific Fleet so it could seize the oil and rubber of Southeast Asia before America could respond. The surprise attack sank or damaged eight battleships and destroyed 188 aircraft; 2,403 Americans were killed. But the fleet's aircraft carriers were at sea, and its fuel tanks and repair yards survived. The attack also ended the debate at home: the America First Committee disbanded within days, and the Senate voted 82 to 0 for war. In the House the vote was 388 to 1; Jeannette Rankin again voted no.

blocks.a: Japan only. The war with Germany began with Germany's declaration three days later.

blocks.html: Many students think the U.S. declared war on Germany first. The U.S. declared war on Japan; Germany declared war on the U.S. three days later. Another slip: Pearl Harbor was the only target. Japan also attacked the Philippines, Guam, Wake Island and British Malaya and Hong Kong the same day.
Pearl Harbor is the start of the U.S. war, not of World War II itself, which began in Europe in 1939 and in China earlier.

blocks.html: After Pearl Harbor, the whole country went to work for the war. More than 16 million Americans served in the armed forces. At home, factories, farms and families were reorganized in months.

Factories switched to war production; millions of women took industrial jobs ("Rosie the Riveter"); rationing, war bonds and scrap drives involved everyone. A. Philip Randolph's planned march on Washington won Executive Order 8802 (1941), banning discrimination in defense industries, and Black Americans pressed a "Double V": victory abroad and at home.

head: Change
Facts
rows: Car plants built tanks and bombers; the U.S. made about 300,000 military aircraft from 1941 to 1945; unemployment fell from about 14 percent (1940) to under 2 percent
Women's share of the labor force rose from about 24 percent to 36 percent (1940 to 1944); over six million women took war jobs; about 350,000 served in uniform
Ration books for sugar, coffee, meat, gasoline and tires; war bonds; victory gardens; scrap metal and rubber drives
Millions moved to war plants in California, Michigan and the South; the Bracero Program (1942) brought Mexican farm workers

blocks.html: Why did civil rights leaders press so hard in wartime? The country was fighting a regime built on racism while practicing segregation at home. In 1941 A. Philip Randolph, head of the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, threatened a march of tens of thousands on Washington. Roosevelt issued Executive Order 8802 in June 1941, and Randolph called off the march. In 1942 the Pittsburgh Courier, a Black newspaper, launched the Double V campaign. About a million Black Americans served, in segregated units; the Tuskegee Airmen flew fighter escorts in Europe, and Navajo code talkers sent messages in the Pacific that the enemy never broke.

Tension came with the change. In 1943 riots broke out in Detroit, and in Los Angeles servicemen attacked young Mexican Americans in the "Zoot Suit Riots." Wartime labor shortages also opened doors that did not fully close after the war.

blocks.title: Change and continuity
blocks.q: Did women's new jobs last after 1945? Use evidence for both sides.
steps: Change that faded: many women were laid off or left factory jobs as veterans returned in 1945 and 1946.
Change that lasted: women's paid work kept rising over the following decades, and many stayed in clerical and service jobs.
So the war was a turning point for some, a pause for others.
blocks.a: Factory jobs mostly ended; the long rise in women's paid work continued.

blocks.html: Many students think women stayed in factory jobs after the war. Many were laid off or left as veterans returned, though women's paid work kept rising over the following decades. A second slip: the armed forces were not integrated in World War II. Desegregation came by Truman's order in 1948.

blocks.html: After Pearl Harbor, fear of a Japanese attack or of sabotage on the West Coast ran high. Long-standing prejudice against Japanese immigrants added to it. Officials, newspapers and farm groups called for removing everyone of Japanese ancestry from the coast.

Executive Order 9066 (February 19, 1942) led to the forced removal of about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry, about two-thirds of them U.S. citizens, to camps. The Supreme Court upheld the removal in Korematsu v. United States (1944). Congress apologized and paid redress in the Civil Liberties Act of 1988.

doc.title: Executive Order 9066 (February 19, 1942)
paras: to prescribe military areas in such places and of such extent as he or the appropriate Military Commander may determine, from which any or all persons may be excluded

marks.note: The order named no group, but it was used against people of Japanese ancestry on the West Coast.

blocks.html: Families had days to sell homes, farms and businesses, often at great loss, and could take only what they could carry. They went first to temporary "assembly centers," some in horse stalls at racetracks, then to ten camps run by the War Relocation Authority in deserts and swamps, behind barbed wire and guard towers. No Japanese American was ever convicted of spying or sabotage for Japan during the war. In Hawaii, where people of Japanese ancestry were a large part of the population, there was no mass removal. Thousands of young men from the camps served in the Army; the 442nd Regimental Combat Team became the most decorated unit of its size in the war.

opts.dissent: Justice Frank Murphy called it the "legalization of racism"; Justices Roberts and Jackson also dissented.
opts.later: Korematsu's conviction was vacated in 1983. In Trump v. Hawaii (2018) Chief Justice Roberts wrote that Korematsu was "gravely wrong the day it was decided."

blocks.html: The Allies agreed to defeat Germany first, since it was the stronger enemy. The home front supplied the weapons; the Soviet Union, which Germany had invaded in June 1941, did most of the fighting on land and suffered the most deaths.

The Allies fought in North Africa (1942), Sicily and Italy (1943), landed in Normandy on D-Day (June 6, 1944) and turned back Germany's last offensive at the Bulge. Germany surrendered on V-E Day (May 8, 1945). Allied soldiers liberated camps where Nazi Germany had murdered six million Jews and millions of others.

blocks.html: Why Africa and Italy before France? The British argued, and Roosevelt agreed, that the Allies were not yet ready to cross the English Channel; landing in North Africa in November 1942 (Operation Torch) got American troops into battle and drove the Germans and Italians out of Africa by May 1943. Sicily (July 1943) and the Italian mainland followed. Meanwhile the Soviets' victory at Stalingrad (ending February 1943) turned the tide in the East. Bombers struck German cities and factories. Then on June 6, 1944, under General Dwight Eisenhower, about 156,000 Allied soldiers landed on five beaches in Normandy. Paris was freed in August. In December 1944 Germany's surprise attack in the Ardennes made a "bulge" in the Allied line; American troops held, and the attack failed by late January.

As Allied armies advanced, they found the camps of the Holocaust. Nazi Germany and its collaborators murdered about six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people, Poles, Soviet prisoners and others. Americans liberated Buchenwald, Dachau and other camps in April 1945. Eisenhower ordered the camps filmed and photographed so no one could later deny what had happened. President Roosevelt died on April 12, 1945; Hitler killed himself on April 30; Germany surrendered on May 8.

blocks.html: After Pearl Harbor, Japan won a string of victories: the Philippines, where thousands of American and Filipino prisoners died on the Bataan Death March (1942), Guam, Wake, Hong Kong, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies. The U.S. fought back across the largest ocean on Earth.

After the turning point at Midway (June 1942), U.S. forces "island hopped" toward Japan (Guadalcanal, Iwo Jima, Okinawa). Atomic bombs struck Hiroshima (August 6, 1945) and Nagasaki (August 9). Japan announced its surrender August 15 and signed it September 2, 1945.

blocks.html: At Midway, American code breakers learned of Japan's plan, and U.S. planes sank four Japanese aircraft carriers in one battle; Japan never regained the initiative. Island hopping meant seizing key islands for airfields and bases while bypassing others, cutting them off. Each step closer to Japan cost more: at Iwo Jima nearly 7,000 Americans were killed, and at Okinawa about 12,000, with far greater Japanese military and civilian losses. Meanwhile the secret Manhattan Project built an atomic bomb, first tested in New Mexico on July 16, 1945. President Harry Truman, who had taken office in April, approved its use after Japan rejected the Allies' call for unconditional surrender.

The bombs killed about 140,000 people in Hiroshima and about 70,000 in Nagasaki by the end of 1945. On August 8 the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. On August 15 Emperor Hirohito announced Japan would surrender; the formal surrender was signed aboard the USS Missouri on September 2.

blocks.html: Even before the war in Europe ended, the Allied leaders met to plan the postwar world. They wanted to avoid the mistakes of 1919, when the U.S. stayed out of the League of Nations.
At Yalta (February 1945) and Potsdam (July 1945) the Allies planned postwar Europe. The United Nations was founded in 1945, with the U.S. as a permanent member of the Security Council.

blocks.html: Why did the U.S. join the UN when it had refused the League? The war had shown that oceans no longer kept America safe, and leaders of both parties now favored joining; the Senate approved the Charter 89 to 2. The UN's Security Council gave five permanent members (the U.S., the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China) a veto, so the great powers would not be outvoted. The Bretton Woods conference (1944) created the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, and the Nuremberg trials (1945 to 1946) tried Nazi leaders for war crimes.

Yalta later became controversial. Critics said Roosevelt gave Eastern Europe to Stalin; defenders answered that Soviet armies already held it and that Stalin's promise of free elections was the most the West could get. Either way, the promise was broken, and disputes over Poland and Germany opened the Cold War.

blocks.html: The wartime allies fell out quickly. The Soviet Union kept its armies in Eastern Europe and installed communist governments there; in 1946 Winston Churchill said an "iron curtain" had descended across the continent. The United States and the Soviet Union, the two superpowers, entered a long rivalry called the Cold War.
The U.S. set out to contain Soviet communism: the Truman Doctrine (1947), the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe (1948), the Berlin Airlift (1948 to 1949) and the NATO alliance (1949).

Diplomat George Kennan argued in 1946 and 1947 that the Soviet Union would expand wherever it could, but could be held back by "vigilant containment of Russian expansive tendencies." When Britain could no longer help Greece and Turkey resist communist pressure, Truman asked Congress for 400 million dollars in aid in March 1947. The Marshall Plan gave about 13 billion dollars to sixteen countries of Western Europe, on the theory that poverty bred communism; the Soviets refused it for themselves and their satellites. When the Soviets blockaded West Berlin in June 1948, the U.S. and Britain flew in food and coal for nearly a year until the blockade was lifted in May 1949. In April 1949, twelve nations formed NATO, pledging that an attack on one is an attack on all. The Soviets answered with their own atomic bomb (1949) and, later, the Warsaw Pact (1955).

blocks.html: As the Cold War deepened, many Americans feared communists inside the country as well as abroad. Like the first Red Scare after World War I, this one mixed real dangers with fear that reached far beyond them.

Fear of Soviet spying (the Hiss and Rosenberg cases) led to loyalty programs, congressional hearings (HUAC) and Senator Joseph McCarthy's accusations (1950 to 1954), until the Senate censured him in December 1954.

The fear had causes. In 1949 the Soviets tested an atomic bomb years sooner than expected, and communists won China's civil war. Alger Hiss, a former State Department official accused of spying, was convicted of perjury in 1950. Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were convicted of passing atomic secrets and executed in 1953. Truman's loyalty program (1947) screened federal workers, and the House Un-American Activities Committee questioned Hollywood writers and others; many were blacklisted and lost their jobs, often for past political ties rather than any crime.

On February 9, 1950, in Wheeling, West Virginia, McCarthy claimed to have a list of communists in the State Department. For four years he made charges he rarely proved, and many people feared to oppose him. In the televised Army-McCarthy hearings of 1954, the Army's lawyer Joseph Welch asked him, "Have you no sense of decency, sir?" Public support fell, and the Senate censured McCarthy, 67 to 22.

Both facts are true: there was spying, and there was an overreach that harmed innocent people.

blocks.html: After World War II, Korea, a Japanese colony since 1910, was divided at the 38th parallel: Soviet troops in the north, American troops in the south. Two governments formed, each claiming the whole country.

North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950. UN forces led by the U.S. fought North Korean and later Chinese armies. An armistice in 1953 left Korea divided near the 38th parallel, with no peace treaty.

blocks.name: cv-timeline

events.label: Inchon landing (September); China enters (October and November)

blocks.cap: Three years of war, then a line close to where it began.

blocks.html: Truman saw the invasion as a test of containment. The UN Security Council, which the Soviets were boycotting, called on members to help South Korea, so this became a UN action with U.S. forces in the lead; Congress never declared war. In September 1950 General Douglas MacArthur's landing at Inchon drove the North Koreans back, and UN forces pushed toward the Chinese border. Then hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops entered and drove them south again. MacArthur publicly called for widening the war against China; Truman relieved him of command in April 1951, upholding civilian control of the military. The war settled into two years of fighting near the 38th parallel while talks went on.

blocks.name: cv-branches
blocks.cap: Congress declares war, but Truman sent troops as commander in chief without a declaration, a precedent later debated in Vietnam.

blocks.title: Counting the cost
blocks.q: About 36,500 Americans died in combat in Korea (some 54,000 military deaths in all, by the official count). Why does a war that ended where it began still matter?
steps: It was the first armed clash of the Cold War and kept South Korea independent.
It led the U.S. to build up its military and keep troops in Asia.
It ended in an armistice, not a treaty, so the two Koreas remain technically at war.
blocks.a: It defended South Korea, expanded the military, and left a divided peninsula.

blocks.html: Many students think the Korean War ended with a peace treaty or a victory. It ended in an armistice (a cease-fire agreement) in July 1953, and Korea remains divided along a demilitarized zone near the 38th parallel.
Truman's firing of MacArthur, a popular war hero, is a classic example of a constitutional principle: the President, an elected civilian, commands the armed forces.
