blocks.html: After Korea, the 1950s brought a long economic boom under President Dwight Eisenhower (1953 to 1961). Many families had money to spend for the first time since the 1920s, and new suburbs, highways and televisions changed daily life.

The GI Bill (1944), suburbs such as Levittown, the baby boom, television and the Interstate Highway Act (1956) reshaped life. The Soviet launch of Sputnik (1957) spurred new spending on science and education.

head: Change
Facts
rows: Paid college tuition and gave low-interest home loans to millions of veterans
Levitt & Sons built about 17,000 houses on Long Island from 1947, mass-produced like cars
In about one home in ten in 1950, in most homes by 1960; shared shows, news and ads
Authorized a 41,000-mile highway system, justified partly for defense
The first satellite; led to NASA and the National Defense Education Act (1958)

blocks.html: Why the boom? The U.S. had come out of the war with its factories whole while Europe and Japan rebuilt. Pent-up savings, cheap mortgages, cars and suburbs fed each other: new houses needed roads, appliances and cars. Defense spending stayed high in the Cold War. In his farewell address in 1961, Eisenhower, a former general, warned against the unchecked influence of a "military-industrial complex."

events.label: Shelley v. Kraemer: courts may not enforce racial covenants

blocks.html: The boom was not shared equally. Levittown's deeds barred sales to non-white buyers, and federal mortgage rules backed "redlining," which marked Black neighborhoods as poor risks. The Supreme Court ruled in 1948 that courts could not enforce racial covenants, but discrimination in lending and sales went on. In 1959 about one American in five lived in poverty, many in rural areas, Appalachia and inner cities.

blocks.title: Following a chain of effects
blocks.q: Trace how the GI Bill and the highways helped build the suburbs.
steps: GI Bill loans let veterans buy homes with little money down.
Builders such as Levitt mass-produced houses on cheap land outside cities.
New highways let suburban workers drive to city jobs.
So the suburbs grew, while many cities lost residents and tax money.
blocks.a: Cheap loans plus mass-built houses plus highways made the suburbs.

blocks.html: Many students think the 1950s were the same for every family. Suburbs often excluded Black families through restrictive covenants and lending practices, and poverty remained in cities and rural areas. The calm image also hides the civil rights struggle of the decade, such as Brown v. Board (1954).

blocks.html: John F. Kennedy, elected in 1960 at 43, promised energy at home and firmness toward the Soviets. The Sputnik shock and a communist revolution in Cuba, 90 miles from Florida, put the Cold War close to home.

The Bay of Pigs invasion failed (1961); the Berlin Wall went up (1961); in the Cuban Missile Crisis (October 1962) the U.S. and the USSR came close to nuclear war before the Soviets removed their missiles; the space race led to Apollo 11's Moon landing (1969).

events.label: Bay of Pigs (April); Moon goal (May); Berlin Wall (August)

blocks.html: In April 1961 about 1,400 Cuban exiles trained by the CIA landed at the Bay of Pigs and were defeated within days. In August the East Germans built a wall through Berlin to stop people escaping to the West. In October 1962 spy planes found Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Kennedy rejected an immediate air strike, set up a naval "quarantine" of Cuba, and demanded the missiles' removal. For thirteen days (October 16 to 28) the world waited. The Soviets agreed to remove the missiles; the U.S. promised not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove its own missiles from Turkey. Afterward the two sides set up a hotline and signed the Limited Test Ban Treaty (1963).

doc.title: John F. Kennedy, special message to Congress (May 25, 1961)
doc.source: Public domain (a work of the U.S. government)
paras: First, I believe that this nation should commit itself to achieving the goal, before this decade is out, of landing a man on the moon and returning him safely to the earth.

marks.note: By the end of the 1960s. Apollo 11 landed on July 20, 1969.

blocks.title: Reading the deal
blocks.q: How did the Cuban Missile Crisis end, and what did each side give?
steps: The Soviets removed their missiles from Cuba, under inspection from the air.
The U.S. publicly promised not to invade Cuba.
The U.S. privately agreed to remove its missiles from Turkey, a part kept secret for years.
blocks.a: A trade: missiles out of Cuba for a no-invasion pledge, plus the secret Turkey deal.

blocks.html: Many students think Kennedy saw the Moon landing. Kennedy set the goal in 1961 and was assassinated in Dallas on November 22, 1963; the landing came on July 20, 1969, under President Nixon. Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above.

blocks.html: Vietnam had been a French colony. Communist-led forces under Ho Chi Minh defeated the French in 1954, and the Geneva Accords divided the country at the 17th parallel. Presidents from Eisenhower on, applying containment and the "domino theory" (if one country fell to communism, its neighbors would follow), backed South Vietnam.

After the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964), U.S. troops in Vietnam grew to over 500,000. The Tet Offensive (1968) shook public support; protests spread at home (Kent State, 1970). The Paris Peace Accords (1973) ended U.S. combat, and Saigon fell in 1975. Congress passed the War Powers Resolution (1973).

doc.title: The Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (August 7, 1964), Section 1
paras: That the Congress approves and supports the determination of the President, as Commander in Chief, to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression.

marks.note: Broad authority to use force, but not a declaration of war.

blocks.html: In August 1964, after reported attacks on U.S. destroyers in the Gulf of Tonkin (the second attack probably did not happen), Congress passed the resolution 416 to 0 in the House and 88 to 2 in the Senate. President Johnson used it to send combat troops and bomb North Vietnam. The war was hard to win: the enemy fought a guerrilla war, was supplied from the North, and could not be defeated by bombing. In January 1968, during the Tet holiday, North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces attacked cities across the South. They were driven back with heavy losses, but the attack made many Americans doubt official claims of progress, and in March Johnson announced he would not run again.

events.label: Paris Peace Accords; War Powers Resolution

blocks.html: President Nixon began "Vietnamization," pulling out U.S. troops while arming South Vietnam, but widened the war into Cambodia in 1970; at Kent State University in Ohio, National Guard troops fired on protesters and killed four students. After the 1973 accords the last U.S. combat troops left. In 1975 North Vietnam conquered the South. About 58,000 Americans died, and Vietnamese deaths ran into the millions.

blocks.title: Why the War Powers Resolution?
blocks.q: Connect the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution to the War Powers Resolution of 1973.
steps: Only Congress can declare war (Article I), but the President is commander in chief (Article II).
In Vietnam, Congress never declared war; a broad resolution let Presidents fight for years.
So in 1973 Congress, over Nixon's veto, required the President to report within 48 hours and withdraw forces after 60 days without its approval.
blocks.a: An undeclared war led Congress to reclaim a check on the war power.

blocks.html: Many students think Congress declared war on Vietnam. It never did; the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution authorized the President to use force, which is why the War Powers Resolution followed. Presidents of both parties have argued that parts of it are unconstitutional, and the debate continues.

blocks.html: Lyndon Johnson became President when Kennedy was assassinated in November 1963. A master of Congress, he won a landslide in 1964 (486 electoral votes to Barry Goldwater's 52) and a large majority in Congress, and set out to finish the work of the New Deal.

Johnson's Great Society (1964 to 1966) included the War on Poverty, Medicare and Medicaid (1965), federal aid to schools, and the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965, which ended the national-origins quotas.

blocks.html: Johnson believed a rich country could end poverty. Michael Harrington's book The Other America (1962) had shown millions of poor Americans whom the suburbs did not see. The official poverty rate fell from about 19 percent in 1964 to about 11 percent in 1973, and poverty among the elderly fell sharply. Supporters credit the programs; critics argue that growth did much of the work, that some programs created dependence or did little, and that costs rose fast. The war in Vietnam drew money and attention away, and riots in many cities from 1965 on and rising inflation weakened support.

blocks.q: How did the 1965 immigration law change the system set up in 1924?
steps: The 1924 law set quotas by national origin, favoring northern and western Europe.
The 1965 law ended national-origins quotas and gave preference to relatives of citizens and to workers with needed skills.
Over the following decades, immigration from Asia and Latin America grew greatly.
blocks.a: It replaced national-origins quotas with family and skill preferences.

blocks.html: Richard Nixon won the presidency in 1968, promising "law and order" and an honorable end to Vietnam. His record mixed bold diplomacy, new domestic programs, and the worst political scandal in American history.

Nixon opened relations with China (1972), signed arms limits with the USSR (SALT I, 1972) and created the EPA (1970). The Watergate scandal and United States v. Nixon (1974) led to his resignation on August 9, 1974.

Détente meant easing tensions with the communist powers. Nixon and his adviser Henry Kissinger used the split between China and the Soviet Union: Nixon visited Beijing in February 1972, then Moscow in May, where he and Leonid Brezhnev signed the SALT I and Anti-Ballistic Missile agreements. At home Nixon signed the Clean Air Act and created the Environmental Protection Agency (1970). In June 1972, men working for his reelection committee were arrested breaking into the Democratic National Committee's offices at the Watergate building. Nixon won reelection in a landslide (520 electoral votes), but reporters, a grand jury and a Senate committee uncovered a cover-up directed from the White House.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.facts: A special prosecutor subpoenaed tape recordings of White House conversations for the trial of Nixon's aides. Nixon refused, claiming executive privilege.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Burger: the courts decide what the law is; a general claim of confidentiality must yield to the specific need for evidence in a criminal trial.

blocks.cap: United States v. Nixon (1974), 8 to 0 (one justice did not take part).

blocks.title: Checks and balances at work
blocks.q: Name a check used by each branch in Watergate.
steps: Legislative: Senate hearings exposed the taping system; the House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment in July 1974.
Judicial: the Supreme Court ordered the tapes released (United States v. Nixon).
The tapes showed Nixon had joined the cover-up days after the break-in; facing certain impeachment and likely removal, he resigned.
blocks.a: Congress investigated and moved to impeach; the Court enforced the subpoena.

blocks.html: Many students think Nixon was impeached and removed. The House Judiciary Committee approved articles of impeachment, but he resigned before the full House voted. Gerald Ford, who had become Vice President under the Twenty-fifth Amendment, became President, and pardoned Nixon a month later.

blocks.name: cv-branches
blocks.cap: The impeachment check: the House charges, the Senate tries.

blocks.html: After the détente of the Nixon years faded with the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (1979), Cold War tension rose again. Within ten years, the Cold War was over, and few had predicted how fast it would end.

Ronald Reagan built up defense and called on the Soviets to "tear down this wall" (1987); he and Mikhail Gorbachev signed the INF Treaty (1987); the Berlin Wall fell (November 9, 1989), and the Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

events.label: Reagan proposes the Strategic Defense Initiative
Revolutions in Eastern Europe; Berlin Wall falls

blocks.html: Reagan called the Soviet Union an "evil empire," raised defense spending and proposed a space-based missile defense. Gorbachev, who took power in 1985, faced a failing economy and a costly war in Afghanistan; he launched glasnost (openness) and perestroika (restructuring). The two leaders met five times; the INF Treaty (December 8, 1987) was the first to eliminate a whole class of nuclear missiles. In 1989 Gorbachev let the peoples of Eastern Europe choose: Poland's Solidarity movement won elections, and on November 9 East Germany opened the Berlin Wall. Germany reunited in 1990. After a failed coup by hard-liners in August 1991, the Soviet republics broke away, and on December 26, 1991, the Soviet Union ceased to exist.

head: Explanation
Evidence its supporters cite
rows: Reagan's military buildup and missile defense plans strained a Soviet economy that could not keep up
Low growth, shortages, falling oil prices and the cost of Afghanistan
Glasnost and perestroika, and his refusal to use force in Eastern Europe in 1989
Solidarity in Poland, mass protests in East Germany and elsewhere
blocks.cap: Historians weigh these together and debate the balance.

INF Treaty: 1987.

blocks.a: 1985, 1987, 1989, 1991: two years apart, easy to remember.

blocks.html: Students credit a single person or cause. Historians weigh U.S. pressure, the Soviet economy's weakness, Gorbachev's reforms and the people of Eastern Europe; they debate the balance. Practice here asks what each explanation argues and when things happened, not which is right.

blocks.html: The civil rights movement did not begin in the 1950s. It built on decades of work by the NAACP, on the votes of Black migrants in Northern cities, and on the Double V campaign of World War II. Black veterans came home from fighting fascism determined to end segregation.

Early victories: Jackie Robinson integrated major league baseball (1947); Truman ordered the armed forces desegregated (1948); Mendez v. Westminster (1947) ended the segregation of Mexican American children in California schools.

head: Year
Victory
Why it mattered
rows: The Supreme Court struck down the "white primary" in Texas
Jackie Robinson joins the Brooklyn Dodgers (April 15)
A national symbol of integration in the most popular sport
Segregating Mexican American children was unlawful; Governor Earl Warren signed a repeal of California's school segregation laws
Equal treatment in the armed forces; the military was largely integrated by the mid-1950s
Courts could not enforce racial covenants in deeds
Texas had to admit a Black student to its law school: a separate school was not equal

blocks.html: Why did progress come first in courts, the military and sports? The NAACP's lawyers, led by Charles Hamilton Houston and then Thurgood Marshall, chose cases carefully, starting with graduate and law schools, where states could not credibly claim that hastily built separate schools were equal. The President could change the military by order, without Congress, where Southern senators blocked civil rights bills by filibuster. Truman's committee report To Secure These Rights (1947) called for an end to segregation; in 1948 some Southern Democrats walked out of their party's convention and ran their own candidate.

blocks.name: cv-timeline
blocks.cap: Decades of groundwork before Montgomery.

blocks.title: Building a legal strategy
blocks.q: Why did the NAACP attack segregation in law schools before attacking it in elementary schools?
steps: Plessy allowed "separate but equal," so the first cases asked whether separate schools were in fact equal.
A state could not build an equal law school, with its faculty, library and alumni, overnight.
Winning those cases (such as Sweatt in 1950) prepared the ground to argue that separation itself is unequal.
blocks.a: Graduate schools were the weakest point of "separate but equal," and each win built a precedent.

blocks.html: Many students think the movement began with Rosa Parks in 1955. Legal and political work went back decades, through the NAACP's lawsuits and wartime campaigns. Another slip: civil rights struggles were only Black and white. Mexican American families won Mendez in 1947, and in Hernandez v. Texas (1954) the Supreme Court held that excluding Mexican Americans from juries violated equal protection.

blocks.html: By the early 1950s the NAACP was ready to challenge Plessy v. Ferguson head on. Five cases from Kansas, South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and the District of Columbia reached the Supreme Court together. Thurgood Marshall argued for the families.

In Brown v. Board of Education (1954) the Supreme Court ruled 9 to 0 that segregated public schools violate the Equal Protection Clause, overturning Plessy for schools. Resistance followed, and in 1957 Eisenhower sent troops to protect the Little Rock Nine.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.facts: Linda Brown and other Black children were required to attend separate schools. In some cases the schools were roughly equal in buildings and teachers; the families argued that separation itself was unequal.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Earl Warren, for a unanimous Court: education is the foundation of good citizenship; separating children by race generates a feeling of inferiority that affects their hearts and minds.

blocks.cap: Brown v. Board of Education (May 17, 1954).

doc.title: Brown v. Board of Education (1954), opinion of Chief Justice Warren
paras: We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of "separate but equal" has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.

marks.note: Unequal by their very nature, even if buildings and teachers were equal.

blocks.html: A unanimous Court mattered: Warren worked to bring every justice along so the South could not point to a divided ruling. But Brown set no timetable. In 1955 (Brown II) the Court told lower courts to desegregate "with all deliberate speed," words that many districts read as permission to delay. In 1956, 101 Southern members of Congress signed the Southern Manifesto against the decision; Virginia's "massive resistance" closed some schools rather than integrate. In September 1957 Arkansas's governor used the National Guard to block nine Black students from Little Rock's Central High School. Eisenhower sent the 101st Airborne Division to escort them, and in Cooper v. Aaron (1958) the Court held that states are bound by its rulings.

events.label: Civil Rights Act lets federal funds be cut off
Green v. County School Board: integrate now

blocks.title: Which clause, which case?
blocks.q: A student writes, "Brown overruled Plessy under the First Amendment." Fix the sentence.
steps: The clause: the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment ("nor deny to any person … the equal protection of the laws").
The scope: Brown rejected "separate but equal" in public education.
Later cases applied the same principle to buses, parks and other public places.
blocks.a: Brown held school segregation violates the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause.

blocks.html: Many students think schools desegregated right after Brown. The Court ordered desegregation "with all deliberate speed" (1955), and many districts resisted for more than a decade. Ten years after Brown, only a small share of Black students in the Deep South attended school with white students; real change came after the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and court orders in the late 1960s.

blocks.html: After Brown, the movement turned to the segregation of daily life. In Montgomery, Alabama, Black riders, most of the city's bus passengers, had to sit in the back and give up seats to white riders on demand.

After Rosa Parks's arrest on December 1, 1955, Black residents of Montgomery boycotted the buses for 381 days, led by Martin Luther King Jr. In 1956 the courts ruled bus segregation unconstitutional (Browder v. Gayle).

Parks was a respected seamstress and the secretary of the local NAACP; she had trained in organizing. When she refused to give up her seat, local leaders were ready. Jo Ann Robinson and the Women's Political Council had planned a boycott and printed tens of thousands of leaflets overnight. E. D. Nixon arranged bail. Ministers formed the Montgomery Improvement Association and chose a 26-year-old pastor, Martin Luther King Jr., as president. For more than a year, about 40,000 people walked, shared rides in a carpool system, or took church station wagons, while the bus company lost most of its riders. King's house was bombed, and leaders were arrested. A federal lawsuit by four other women, Browder v. Gayle, ended segregation on the buses: the Supreme Court affirmed on November 13, 1956, and the boycott ended on December 20.

blocks.title: Why did it work?
blocks.q: Name two reasons the Montgomery boycott succeeded.
steps: Economic pressure: Black riders were most of the bus company's customers, so the boycott cost it heavily.
Organization: planning by the Women's Political Council, a carpool system and support from churches kept it going for 381 days.
Law: the federal lawsuit gave the boycott a legal victory to end on.
blocks.a: Economic pressure, careful organization and a winning lawsuit.

blocks.html: Many students think the boycott was spontaneous, or that Parks was simply too tired to move. Local leaders and groups, including the Women's Political Council, had planned for such a protest and organized carpools to keep it going; Parks was an experienced activist. Others, such as 15-year-old Claudette Colvin earlier in 1955, had also refused to give up their seats.

blocks.html: The Montgomery boycott showed what organized, nonviolent protest could do. In the early 1960s a new generation, many of them college students, carried it across the South.

Students sat in at a Greensboro lunch counter (1960) and founded SNCC; Freedom Riders tested bus integration (1961); after the Birmingham campaign (1963) and King's "Letter from Birmingham Jail," about 250,000 people joined the March on Washington (August 28, 1963).

When
What happened

Students met at Shaw University with guidance from Ella Baker

blocks.html: Nonviolent protest was a strategy, not just a moral choice. Protesters were trained, in workshops such as James Lawson's in Nashville, to sit quietly, dress well and not strike back when cursed, burned with cigarettes or beaten. That discipline exposed the violence of segregation to the nation, and to the world in the middle of the Cold War, and pushed the federal government to act. In his letter from the Birmingham jail (April 16, 1963), King answered eight white clergymen who had called the protests unwise and untimely. He argued that people have a moral duty to disobey unjust laws and that, for Black Americans, being told to wait had almost always meant never. That fall a bomb at the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham killed four girls.

blocks.title: Tactic and target
blocks.q: Match each tactic to what it targeted: sit-in; Freedom Ride; march.
steps: Sit-in: segregated lunch counters and stores, by occupying seats.
Freedom Ride: segregated interstate buses and terminals, by riding them.
March: public opinion and Congress, by gathering in great numbers.
blocks.a: Sit-ins targeted stores, Freedom Rides targeted travel, marches targeted the nation and its laws.

blocks.html: Many students think nonviolent protest meant passive protest. It was organized, trained and risky: protesters planned carefully, practiced not striking back, and faced arrests, beatings and bombings. The point was to act, and to make injustice visible.

blocks.html: The protests of 1960 to 1963 pushed civil rights to the top of the national agenda. President Kennedy proposed a civil rights bill in June 1963. After his assassination, Lyndon Johnson made its passage his first priority.

The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned discrimination in public places and jobs; the Twenty-fourth Amendment (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections; after the Selma marches, the Voting Rights Act (1965) ended literacy tests and brought federal oversight; the Fair Housing Act followed in 1968.

Signed
Main provisions
rows: Title II: no discrimination in hotels, restaurants and other public accommodations; Title VI: no discrimination in programs with federal money; Title VII: no job discrimination by race, color, religion, sex or national origin
No poll tax in federal elections (Harper v. Virginia, 1966, ended state poll taxes)

blocks.html: Passing the 1964 act took a long fight. Southern senators filibustered for 60 working days until a bipartisan coalition, with key support from Republican leader Everett Dirksen, voted cloture to end debate. Voting came next. In 1964, during Freedom Summer, volunteers registered voters in Mississippi, where only about 6.7 percent of eligible Black citizens were registered; three civil rights workers were murdered. On March 7, 1965, state troopers beat marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, Alabama ("Bloody Sunday"). Johnson went before Congress, and the Voting Rights Act passed that summer. Black registration in the South rose sharply within a few years.

blocks.name: cv-bill
blocks.cap: The Civil Rights Act took the ordinary path, with one hard step: ending a Senate filibuster.

blocks.title: Which law applies?
blocks.q: A restaurant in 1965 refuses to serve Black customers; a county keeps a literacy test for voters. Which law covers each?
steps: Restaurants are public accommodations: Title II of the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
Literacy tests for voting: the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
The Supreme Court upheld Title II under the Commerce Clause (Heart of Atlanta Motel, 1964).
blocks.a: The restaurant: the 1964 act. The literacy test: the 1965 act.

blocks.html: Students mix up the 1964 and 1965 laws. The Civil Rights Act (1964) covered public places and jobs; the Voting Rights Act (1965) covered voting. Memory aid: public places and jobs came first (1964), the ballot box a year later (1965). A later fact: in Shelby County v. Holder (2013) the Supreme Court struck down the formula that chose which states needed preclearance.

blocks.html: The great civil rights laws ended legal segregation in the South, but they did not end poverty, police violence or segregated housing in Northern cities. In the mid-1960s the movement argued openly about its goals and methods. Each position grew from real experience; understanding them means hearing each on its own terms.
Leaders differed on methods and goals: King's nonviolent integration, Malcolm X's call for self-defense and Black pride, and the Black Power movement (from 1966). King was assassinated in April 1968.

Malcolm X

At first, separation and Black self-reliance (Nation of Islam); later, human rights for Black people worldwide

blocks.html: Why did the debate sharpen after 1965? Riots broke out in Watts (Los Angeles) in 1965 and in Newark, Detroit and other cities in 1967. The Kerner Commission (1968) warned that the nation was "moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal." Many young activists, beaten and jailed in the South, doubted that nonviolence and white allies could win. In June 1966, during a march in Mississippi, Stokely Carmichael of SNCC called for "Black Power." King, meanwhile, turned to poverty and spoke against the Vietnam War. He was killed in Memphis on April 4, 1968, while supporting striking sanitation workers.

Malcolm X's views changed late in his life. After leaving the Nation of Islam in March 1964 and making the pilgrimage to Mecca, he spoke of working with others, including some white allies, for human rights. He was assassinated on February 21, 1965.

blocks.title: Describing, not judging
blocks.q: Write one fair sentence for each side of the debate over nonviolence.
steps: For nonviolence: disciplined protest exposed the brutality of segregation and won national laws.
For self-defense: people facing bombings and beatings had a right to protect themselves, and nonviolence had not changed conditions in Northern cities.
Both sides wanted equal rights and dignity; they differed on means and on integration as the goal.
blocks.a: Each side, in its own terms; no verdict needed.

blocks.html: Students reduce the debate to "good" and "bad" leaders. Present each leader's argument in his own terms and the circumstances behind it; Malcolm X's views also changed late in his life. King himself grew more critical of poverty and war, and the Black Power movement included community programs as well as rhetoric.

blocks.html: The civil rights movement gave other groups a model: organize, protest, go to court, and press Congress. In the 1960s and 1970s farmworkers, Native nations, women and people with disabilities all drew on it.

Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta organized farmworkers (the UFW); the American Indian Movement (1968) pressed for treaty rights; the women's movement won Title IX (1972), though the Equal Rights Amendment was not ratified; the Americans with Disabilities Act passed in 1990.

blocks.html: Title IX (1972) said that no one could be excluded on the basis of sex from any education program receiving federal money; girls' and women's school sports grew enormously as a result. The Equal Rights Amendment said that equality of rights under the law shall not be denied on account of sex. Congress passed it in March 1972 by large bipartisan majorities, and many states ratified quickly. Then opposition grew, led by Phyllis Schlafly, who argued it would harm women by ending legal protections such as exemption from the draft; supporters argued it would secure equality that ordinary laws could change. By the extended deadline of 1982, 35 states had ratified, three short of the 38 needed.

blocks.title: Is the ERA in the Constitution?
blocks.q: Use Article V to explain the ERA's status.
steps: Article V: an amendment proposed by Congress takes effect when three-fourths of the states ratify (38 of 50).
Congress set a deadline, extended to 1982; 35 states had ratified by then, and five had voted to rescind.
Three more states ratified later (2017 to 2020). Whether those count, after the deadline, is disputed; it has not been certified as part of the Constitution.
blocks.a: Not ratified by the deadline; its status is disputed.

blocks.html: Many students think the Equal Rights Amendment is part of the Constitution. Congress passed it in 1972, but it was not ratified by three-fourths of the states before its deadline, and its status remains disputed. Another mix-up: Title IX is a law, not an amendment, and covers far more than sports.

blocks.html: After Watergate and the end of the Vietnam War, many Americans lost trust in government. At the same time the long postwar boom ended. The 1970s brought problems that the tools of earlier decades did not seem to fix.

An oil embargo (1973) and "stagflation" (high inflation with high unemployment) strained the economy. Gerald Ford pardoned Nixon. Jimmy Carter brokered the Camp David Accords (1978) and faced the Iran hostage crisis (1979 to 1981).

In October 1973, during a war between Israel and its neighbors, Arab oil-producing nations cut off oil to the United States, and the price of crude oil roughly quadrupled, from about 3 dollars to about 12 dollars a barrel. Gasoline lines formed, and prices rose across the economy. Economists had expected inflation and unemployment to move in opposite directions; now both were high at once. Ford's pardon of Nixon in September 1974, meant to put Watergate behind the country, cost him trust, and Carter, a former Georgia governor who ran as an outsider, won in 1976. A second oil shock in 1979 pushed inflation above 13 percent by 1980; the Federal Reserve under Paul Volcker then raised interest rates sharply to bring it down.

blocks.title: Reading two numbers at once
blocks.q: In 1974 inflation was about 11 percent and in 1975 unemployment reached about 9 percent. Why did this puzzle policymakers?
steps: The usual tool against unemployment, more spending or cheaper money, tends to raise inflation.
The usual tool against inflation, less spending or higher interest rates, tends to raise unemployment.
With both high at once, each cure seemed to worsen the other problem.
blocks.a: Stagflation: the standard remedies pulled in opposite directions.

blocks.html: Many students think inflation and unemployment always move in opposite directions. In the 1970s both were high at once, which puzzled policymakers. Economists still debate the causes: the oil shocks, earlier spending and loose money, and rising expectations of inflation all figure.

blocks.html: The troubles of the 1970s opened the way for a political shift. A conservative movement that had grown since Barry Goldwater's campaign of 1964, with think tanks, magazines and new religious groups such as the Moral Majority (1979), found its leader in a former actor and governor of California.

Ronald Reagan won in 1980 and 1984 on lower taxes, less regulation and a stronger defense. Supporters credit his policies with the long expansion after 1982, while critics point to larger deficits and widening inequality.

blocks.name: cv-ec
blocks.cap: An electoral vote calculator on today's map. In 1980 Reagan won 489 of 538 electoral votes; in 1984 he won 525, the most ever.

head: Policy
What was done
rows: The Economic Recovery Tax Act (1981) cut income tax rates by about a quarter; the top rate fell from 70 to 50 percent. The Tax Reform Act (1986), passed with bipartisan votes, lowered the top rate to 28 percent and closed many deductions
Fewer and lighter federal rules for business and energy; air traffic controllers who struck illegally in 1981 were fired
A large military buildup and the Strategic Defense Initiative (1983)
The Federal Reserve kept interest rates high; inflation fell from about 13.5 percent (1980) to under 4 percent by 1983, after a deep recession in 1981 and 1982

blocks.html: What does the record show? Unemployment peaked at 10.8 percent in late 1982, then fell to about 5.3 percent by 1989, during an expansion that lasted until 1990. Federal deficits grew, and the national debt roughly tripled during the decade, since spending, especially on defense and entitlements, rose while tax rates fell. Incomes rose fastest at the top. Supporters argue that lower tax rates and less regulation released growth and that the buildup helped end the Cold War; critics argue that the deficits burdened the future and that the gains were unevenly shared. Reagan also appointed Sandra Day O'Connor, the first woman on the Supreme Court (1981).

blocks.title: Facts first, then readings
blocks.q: Separate the facts from the judgments: "Taxes were cut in 1981. The cuts caused the boom. The debt tripled. The deficits were dangerous."
steps: Facts: tax rates were cut in 1981 (and again in 1986); the national debt roughly tripled in the 1980s.
Judgments: that the cuts caused the boom (supporters' reading), and that the deficits were dangerous (critics' reading).
A historian states the facts and then each side's reading, with its evidence.
blocks.a: Two facts, two interpretations.

blocks.html: Students state one side's judgment as fact. Describe the policies and the record (tax cuts in 1981 and 1986, rising deficits, falling inflation), then each side's reading of them. Words like "success" or "failure" belong to the debate, not to the facts.

blocks.html: With the Soviet Union gone by the end of 1991, the United States was the world's only superpower. Presidents George H. W. Bush (1989 to 1993) and Bill Clinton (1993 to 2001) had to decide when and how to use that power.

The U.S. led a coalition in the Gulf War (1991), joined NAFTA (in force 1994), took part in NATO operations in Bosnia (1995) and Kosovo (1999), and faced new questions about its role as the only superpower.

events.label: Gulf War: Desert Storm (January to February)
NAFTA takes effect; genocide in Rwanda
NATO air strikes in Bosnia; Dayton Accords

blocks.html: When Iraq's Saddam Hussein invaded Kuwait in August 1990, Bush built a coalition of about 35 nations, won a UN Security Council resolution, and asked Congress to authorize force, which it did in January 1991. Operation Desert Storm began with an air campaign on January 17, 1991; a ground war of about 100 hours freed Kuwait, and a cease-fire came on February 28. Later in the decade the questions were harder. In Somalia, a mission to feed famine victims turned into fighting, and U.S. troops left after 18 soldiers were killed in Mogadishu in 1993. In 1994 the world, including the U.S., did not intervene as hundreds of thousands of people were killed in Rwanda. In the former Yugoslavia, NATO air strikes in 1995 helped bring the Dayton Accords for Bosnia, and in 1999 a 78-day NATO air campaign forced Serbian forces out of Kosovo.

Trade linked the economies. The North American Free Trade Agreement, signed in 1992 and passed by Congress in 1993 with votes from both parties, took effect January 1, 1994, removing most tariffs among the U.S., Canada and Mexico. The World Trade Organization followed in 1995. Supporters pointed to cheaper goods and growing exports; opponents, including many labor unions, warned of lost manufacturing jobs.

blocks.title: Comparing two interventions
blocks.q: How did the Gulf War (1991) differ from the Kosovo campaign (1999)?
steps: Gulf War: the UN Security Council authorized force, Congress voted to authorize it, and a large ground war freed Kuwait.
Kosovo: NATO acted without a new UN Security Council resolution, by air power alone, to stop attacks on civilians.
Both were coalitions led by the U.S.
blocks.a: UN-authorized ground war versus NATO air war.

blocks.html: Many students think the end of the Cold War ended American military actions abroad. The 1990s saw several deployments under the UN and NATO: the Gulf, Somalia, Haiti, Bosnia and Kosovo. Americans debated each one, and whether the country should act as a world police force at all.

blocks.html: While politics in the 1990s focused on a world after the Cold War, a quieter revolution changed daily life. Computers moved from government labs and big companies into homes, schools and pockets.

Personal computers spread in the 1980s; the World Wide Web (1991) opened the internet to the public; trade and investment linked economies worldwide, and the country debated the gains and costs of globalization.

blocks.html: Why did the new technology matter so much? Chips kept getting cheaper and more powerful, so machines that once filled rooms fit on desks. The internet let any computer exchange data with any other; the Web added pages linked to each other that anyone could read with a browser. Businesses could coordinate factories, offices and suppliers around the world, which helped drive globalization: the growing flow of goods, money, people and ideas across borders. Supporters of globalization pointed to cheaper goods, new markets and growth; critics pointed to factory jobs moved overseas and to towns that lost their main employer. Both effects were real, and they fell on different people.

The internet grew from 1960s and 1970s research networks; the Web is a system of linked pages that runs on it, created in 1989 to 1991. Email, for example, used the internet long before the Web.

blocks.html: The conservative resurgence changed both parties. In 1992 Bill Clinton, governor of Arkansas, ran as a "New Democrat" who would pursue growth and smaller deficits. A three-way race followed: Clinton won 370 electoral votes, President George H. W. Bush 168, and independent Ross Perot none, though Perot won about 19 percent of the popular vote.

Bill Clinton (1993 to 2001) signed NAFTA and a 1996 welfare reform passed by a Republican Congress; the federal budget ran surpluses from 1998 to 2001; the House impeached Clinton in 1998 and the Senate acquitted him in 1999; the 2000 election was decided after Bush v. Gore.

Clinton's plan for national health insurance failed in 1994, and that fall Republicans, campaigning on Newt Gingrich's "Contract with America," won the House for the first time since 1954. Divided government brought clashes, including two government shutdowns in 1995 and 1996, and also compromises. The welfare law of 1996 replaced a federal entitlement with block grants to states (TANF), with work requirements and a five-year lifetime limit on federal benefits. With a growing economy, tax increases in 1993, and spending limits, the budget showed a surplus in the fiscal years 1998 to 2001, the first since 1969.

blocks.name: cv-ec
blocks.cap: The 2000 result: Bush 271, Gore 266. Gore won the national popular vote by about half a million votes.

blocks.html: In 1998 an independent counsel's investigation led the House to impeach Clinton on charges of perjury and obstruction of justice, arising from testimony in a civil lawsuit. In the Senate trial, neither article came close to the two-thirds needed to remove him (45 and 50 votes to convict). Then the 2000 election came down to Florida, where Bush led by a few hundred votes. On December 12, 2000, in Bush v. Gore, the Supreme Court stopped the recount: seven justices found that the varying recount standards raised an equal protection problem, and five held that no fair recount could be finished in time. Bush won Florida's electoral votes by 537 votes and became President.

blocks.title: How impeachment works
blocks.q: Use the Constitution to trace Clinton's case.
steps: Article I, Section 2: the House has the sole power of impeachment; it voted to impeach in December 1998.
Article I, Section 3: the Senate tries the case, with the Chief Justice presiding, and two-thirds (67 senators) must vote to convict.
The Senate voted 45 and 50 to convict on the two articles in February 1999, so Clinton was acquitted.
blocks.a: Impeached by the House, acquitted by the Senate, like Andrew Johnson in 1868.

blocks.html: Many students think impeachment means removal from office. The House impeaches (charges) and the Senate holds the trial; Clinton, like Andrew Johnson, was acquitted. Removal requires a two-thirds vote of the Senate, which has never happened to a President.

blocks.html: You have now studied American history from the first peoples to 2000, in U.S. History I and this course. The AP U.S. History course divides that story into nine periods. Knowing them gives every event a home, and makes it easier to explain how one era led to the next.

Anchor each period with its start date and one or two events: 1491, 1607, 1754, 1800, 1844, 1865, 1890, 1945, 1980. Then place events in their periods and in order, and link a cause in one period to an effect in the next.

blocks.html: Why do the periods overlap? Historians draw periods by themes, not just by dates. Period 5 runs to 1877 to finish Reconstruction, while Period 6 starts in 1865 to begin the story of industry and the West, which started during the war. In the same way, 1890 to 1898 belongs to both the Gilded Age (Period 6) and the age of empire and reform (Period 7). An event in an overlap can be placed in either, depending on the theme.

steps: Cause: the Depression led to the New Deal and a larger federal role in the economy (1930s).
Effect: after 1945, Americans expected the federal government to manage the economy and provide a safety net; the Great Society (1964 to 1966) expanded it.
The link: a new idea of government's job carried from one period to the next.
